title: Compile is not a passing test
prompt: Explain each command and flag. A simv executable exists, but no PASS message appears. What evidence would establish a successful simulation?
artifact:
tcsh
source ~/EE5327.cshrc
vcs -full64 -Mupdate -debug_access+all -kdb fa_st.v fa_gate.v
./simv -gui
# Log ends: simulation stopped at time 0
hint: Build success establishes something different from a scoreboard passing.
solution: tcsh starts the C shell; source loads the course environment into that shell. The space after source is required. Prompt characters depend on shell configuration.

VCS compiles HDL, elaborates the hierarchy, and builds simv. -full64 selects 64-bit operation; -Mupdate enables incremental compilation; -debug_access+all enables broad debug visibility; -kdb generates the debug database used by Verdi.

./simv -gui launches simulation with a supported GUI; the installed configuration determines GUI integration. Check the selected testbench top, stimulus, clock, reset, run command, and termination condition.
Require actual comparisons, an executed test count, a failure count of zero, and a reachable PASS condition. A waveform or executable alone is insufficient.
rubric: Distinguishes compilation, elaboration, and execution.
Explains every supplied flag without calling -kdb a simulation result.
Names at least three causes of a time-zero stop.
Defines objective pass/fail evidence.
followups: How would you prove your checker can fail?
Why might incremental compilation reuse stale results if the flow or file list is wrong?
theory: Elaboration resolves modules, parameters, and hierarchy.
A simulation can complete successfully while testing nothing.
sources: User-provided VCS/server notes; foundations extension (Labs 1–2 not attached).

title: Read the virtual-clock budget
prompt: Find the maximum internal input-to-output delay and slack for this purely combinational block. Explain what the virtual clock represents. Assume ns and no other uncertainty or latency.
artifact:
create_clock -name CLK -period 1
set_input_delay 0.08 -clock CLK [all_inputs]
set_output_delay 0.12 -clock CLK [all_outputs]

Synthetic max-path report:
input external delay      0.08
combinational delay       0.52
data arrival time         0.60
data required time        0.88
hint: Required time minus arrival time is setup slack.
solution: The internal budget is 1.00 − 0.08 − 0.12 = 0.80 ns.
The external input delay contributes to arrival time; output delay reserves time for the receiving external path. Neither inserts a physical gate into the design.
Slack is 0.88 − 0.60 = +0.28 ns. The virtual clock has no attached design port and provides a timing reference for external I/O relationships.
rubric: Calculates 0.80 ns internal budget.
Calculates +0.28 ns slack.
Explains input/output delay as external timing budgets.
Explains why a combinational design can have a timing clock.
followups: What changes when you add clock uncertainty?
What additional information is needed to check a minimum-delay path?
theory: A clock period is expressed in the timing library/tool time unit.
A virtual clock does not create flip-flops or a physical clock tree.
sources: Lab 3, pp. 12–13 and virtual-clock question on p. 20.

title: Timing load is not an I/O delay
prompt: Explain what each constraint models. Predict why changing the load can worsen timing even though the output-delay value stays fixed. Identify a risk in the wildcard library-pin lookup.
artifact:
set_driving_cell -lib_cell BUFFD2BWP20P90 \
  -input_transition_rise 0.1 -input_transition_fall 0.1 [all_inputs]
set_load [expr {[load_of [get_lib_pins */BUFFD2BWP20P90/I]] * 4}] [all_outputs]
set_output_delay 0.12 -clock CLK [all_outputs]
hint: One describes the source, one the electrical destination, and one the external time budget.
solution: set_driving_cell models an external source cell; it helps estimate input slew and load-dependent source behavior. The transition options describe the transition at the driving cell input, not a physical buffer inserted inside the block.
set_load assigns external capacitance; here it is four times the referenced input-pin capacitance. Check units and ensure the query resolves the intended single pin.
set_output_delay reserves external timing budget. Increasing capacitance can increase final-stage delay and slew, causing resizing or buffering even when the time budget is unchanged.
A wildcard can match several libraries or corners. Use a fully qualified library/pin and verify the collection before applying the constraint.
rubric: Separates electrical loading from timing budgets.
Does not claim set_driving_cell inserts a buffer.
Predicts delay/slew effects and possible area/power cost.
Detects ambiguous wildcard results.
followups: Why should clocks usually be excluded from a blanket data-input driver constraint?
How would you detect a result obtained with an unrealistically weak or strong driver?
theory: Cell delay depends on input transition and output load.
Report units before interpreting capacitance numbers.
sources: Lab 3, driver/load constraints sections.

title: Nine states: binary or one-hot?
prompt: Compute the minimum binary state-register width and compare the candidates. The output interface requires nonnegative slack in every path group. Explain whether one-hot is automatically better.

Encoding  State FFs  Total area  Output slack  Reg2reg slack
Binary        4        30.0       +0.04 ns       -0.03 ns

title: Prove two FSM states equivalent

Input x | A: output,next | B: output,next | C: output,next

   1    |      1,D       |      1,D       |      1,E
D and E are behaviorally distinguishable.
Reset enters A. No externally visible state-debug port.

title: Reset changed the hardware
prompt: Explain the behavioral and mapped-cell difference. Design a short test that distinguishes these two modules without waiting for a rising clock edge.
hint: Notice both the sensitivity list and the reset value.
solution: A has an asynchronous active-low control that sets q to 1; B has synchronous reset-to-one behavior. Do not call A an asynchronous clear-to-zero.
Drive q to 0, then assert rst_n low between clock edges. After the nonblocking update, A becomes 1 immediately; B remains 0 until the next rising edge.
Mapping depends on available cells: A needs suitable asynchronous set/preset behavior; B can use a synchronous-control cell or a data-input mux. Inspect mapped cells and schematics.
Check asynchronous reset deassertion recovery/removal and the reset-release strategy; simulation of RTL alone does not establish metastability safety.
rubric: Distinguishes async versus sync behavior.

Provides a between-edge test.

title: Functional coverage is not fault coverage
prompt: Compute fault coverage and test coverage using the stated definitions. Explain why neither proves the RTL meets its specification.
artifact:
Synthetic ATPG summary (no partially detected faults):
Detected faults                       282
Proven undetectable faults              16
Other undetected faults                 0
Total faults                          298

For this exercise:
fault coverage = detected / total
test coverage = detected / (total − proven undetectable)
hint: The denominator changes; the design behavior has not been proved.
solution: Manufacturing fault coverage measures detection under a specified fault model, such as stuck-at or transition. Functional coverage measures exercised behaviors in a verification plan.

A perfect score within one fault model does not prove absence of every physical defect, and neither ATPG score proves functional correctness. Always report the fault model, exclusions, and coverage definitions.
rubric: Calculates both percentages with the right denominators.
Distinguishes functional coverage from manufacturing fault coverage.

followups: Why might two tools report different test coverage for the same raw counts?

theory: ATPG needs controllability and observability.
Coverage metrics require definitions and classification rules, especially with partially detected faults.
sources: Lab 6, pp. 21–23 sample coverage reports.

title: A scan-chain off-by-one
prompt: Write a checker for this four-bit scan chain. Define bit order, shifting, capture, and observation timing before coding. Show the expected shifted-out sequence for the initial state.
hint: Each observation is the old most-significant bit, not the value after shifting.
solution: The observed sequence is 1,0,1,1. After all four shifts, q is 0011.
Maintain a four-bit software/model register. Before each shift edge compare scan_out with model[3], then update model = {model[2:0], scan_in}.
For capture, deassert scan_en, drive functional_d, allow one functional edge, and set the model to the captured data. Then resume shifting and compare the resulting bits.
Avoid testbench races by driving away from the active edge and sampling with a defined timing discipline. Include all-zero/all-one, alternating, capture, and reset interactions.

title: Why clk AND enable is unsafe
prompt: Explain the hazard and propose a synthesis-friendly replacement. State what you would verify after clock-gating insertion.
hint: What does gclk do at 7 ns?
solution: gclk rises at 7 ns, creating an unintended edge and a shortened pulse. A combinational AND does not guarantee glitch-free clock gating.
Describe a clock enable in RTL: always_ff @(posedge clk) if (enable) q <= d;. Let the supported synthesis flow infer qualified integrated clock-gating cells.
For a positive-edge clock, a typical latch-based ICG holds the enable stable during the high phase. Use the library cell and its test control, rather than hand-building a clock gate.
Check functional equivalence, clock-gating setup/hold checks, gated-register coverage, scan/test behavior, generated clock propagation, and post-CTS timing/power.
rubric: Identifies the unintended 7 ns rising edge.

followups: How does test enable allow scan shifting through a gated clock domain?

title: Clock gating break-even
prompt: Estimate the minimum idle fraction at which gating saves dynamic power, using the stated simplified model. List effects excluded from this estimate.
artifact:
Synthetic energy model per source-clock cycle:
Ungated register bank clock energy:        20 pJ
ICG overhead, every source cycle:            2 pJ
When active, bank still consumes:           20 pJ
When idle, bank clock energy becomes:        0 pJ
Ignore leakage and enable-transition overhead.
Let idle fraction = p.
hint: Compare 20 with 2 + 20(1−p).
solution: Ungated energy is 20 pJ/cycle. Gated energy is 2 + 20(1−p) = 22−20p pJ/cycle.
Gating saves energy when 22−20p < 20, so p > 0.10. The break-even idle fraction is 10%; exactly 10% produces no savings.

The model excludes leakage, enable logic/activity, clock-tree redistribution, capacitance changes, wakeup behavior, and timing/test overhead. Validate with representative activity and implementation reports.
rubric: Derives both energy expressions.
Calculates 10% break-even and strict saving above it.
Distinguishes energy/cycle from average power.
Names at least three omitted physical effects.
followups: How does grouping more registers under one gate affect break-even and enable granularity?
What happens if the enable net itself has high fanout and activity?
theory: Clock gating has overhead and is workload-dependent.
Energy per source cycle multiplied by source frequency gives average power for this model.
sources: Lab 7 clock-gating concepts; original quantitative extension.

numeric.label: Break-even idle fraction
numeric.explanation: 22 − 20p = 20 gives p = 0.10; savings require more than 10%.

title: Sort timing reports numerically
prompt: Write Tcl that discovers all matching reg2reg reports, extracts the first slack in each, and prints filenames with slack sorted worst-first. Skip missing slack with a warning; do not hard-code file names or implement your own sort.
artifact:
Synthetic files under ./reports/:
a.timing.reg2reg.rpt: slack (VIOLATED) -0.12
b.timing.reg2reg.rpt: slack (MET)       0.03
c.timing.reg2reg.rpt: slack (VIOLATED) -2.0e-2
d.timing.reg2reg.rpt: No paths.
Expected order: a, c, b; warning for d.
hint: Use glob -nocomplain, a numeric regex, and lsort -real -index.
solution: Discover reports with glob; preserve filenames as Tcl list elements so spaces are safe. Extract the first slack in each report, matching the exercise contract.
Use lsort -real -index 0 on pairs of {slack filename}; dictionary/string sorting gives the wrong numeric ordering.
Warn and skip reports without a usable slack value; an empty/no-path report must not silently become zero. Production flows may instead fail when a required group has no paths.
This assignment appears at the end of Lab 7 but the handout says it is submitted in Lab 8.
rubric: Discovers any number of matching reports.
Parses signed/scientific notation slack.
Uses built-in numeric sorting.
Reports missing values explicitly.
Keeps filenames and numeric slack associated.
followups: When would taking the first slack be wrong?
How would you extend this to compare corners without mixing time units?
theory: A report can be missing because the design or constraints changed.
Sort by numeric value, not formatted text.

title: Interrogate a clock-gating report
prompt: Calculate gated-register coverage. Decide what additional evidence is needed before calling the run successful; explain at least three reasons some registers remain ungated.
artifact:
Synthetic clock-gating summary:
Total registers                   128
Registers controlled by ICGs       96
Registers not clock gated          32
Inserted ICG cells                  4

Same-frequency power:
Before: internal 8 mW, switching 3 mW, leakage 1 mW
After:  internal 5 mW, switching 2 mW, leakage 1.2 mW
Worst setup slack after: -0.03 ns
hint: A power reduction does not erase a timing failure.
solution: Gated-register coverage is 96/128 = 75%. Total reported power falls from 12 to 8.2 mW, but the timing violation makes the implementation infeasible under the current requirement.

Ungated registers might lack a common enable, be always active, fall below a grouping threshold, be excluded by constraints, or be incompatible with available gating cells/test requirements. Inspect the actual reasons.
Check equivalence, activity quality, gate-enable timing, scan behavior, all timing groups/corners, and physical implementation effects. Coverage alone is not saved-power percentage.
rubric: Computes 75% coverage.
Rejects a timing-failing solution despite lower power.
Names three plausible ungated-register causes.
Separates gating coverage from power savings.
followups: Would you gate a two-register bank? What determines the answer?
Why might one ICG serving many registers be a physical timing problem?
theory: Clock-gating reports describe structural insertion, not workload usefulness.
Dynamic power is internal plus switching power in this report convention.
sources: Lab 7, pp. 14–16 clock-gating and power reports.

title: Defend your optimization experiment
prompt: You are asked in an interview: “What did you design, and how do you know your improvement is real?” Build a 90-second answer from these results. Identify the missing evidence before making a final claim.
artifact:
Synthetic same-frequency, same-corner results:
                    Baseline    Candidate
Cell area              100         108
Dynamic power          12 mW        8 mW
Leakage                 1 mW      1.3 mW
Worst setup slack    +0.05 ns    +0.01 ns
Functional tests        20          20
Equivalence status     n/a        not run
Activity annotation    96%         62%
Post-route results     none        none
hint: Start with requirements, then the decision and tradeoff; do not turn uncertain measurements into achievements.
solution: State the requirement and proposed mechanism: reduce clock-related dynamic power while preserving behavior and timing, accepting some cell-area overhead.
Report the observed tradeoff: area +8%, nominal total power 13→9.3 mW, and reduced setup margin. Do not claim a validated 28.46% saving because activity coverage changed substantially.
Repair/match activity annotation, add targeted tests and equivalence where available, inspect hold/electrical checks, and compare consistent physical stages and corners.
Describe alternatives considered, such as clock-enable grouping, selective Vt, or datapath changes; justify the chosen method with measurements and acknowledge no post-route signoff yet.
rubric: States requirements and the optimization mechanism.
Quantifies costs as well as benefits.
Identifies activity mismatch and missing equivalence evidence.
Explains alternative choices and follow-up validation.
Avoids presenting synthesis estimates as measured silicon.
followups: Which failure would make you abandon clock gating and try a different approach?
What would you measure first if post-route power contradicted synthesis?
How would you explain the tradeoff to someone owning the system power budget?
theory: Interview strength comes from decisions, alternatives, evidence, and limits.
Equal test counts do not imply equal or sufficient functional coverage.
